summary:
A fuzzy protein search finds an approximate motif: X matches any residue, B, Z and J their ambiguous pairs. It returns matches found, fewest mismatches in a hit and residues searched, and the panel shows all of them at once.

Every hit is reported with its position, its mass and how many positions it missed — the quick way to find a motif in a protein whose exact sequence you are not sure of. Press Calculate and the results appear in the grey boxes; after the first press they keep up with every edit, so there is no page to reload. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: How do I use the Fuzzy Protein Search?
sections.html:
Every input sits in the same order the formula is written, so the page reads like the equation.

  1. Paste the protein and the motif. Case does not matter.
  2. Allow a mismatch or two if the sequence comes from a different isoform or a related species.
  3. Read the positions and the reported masses: the mass tells you at a glance whether the hit is the peptide you expect or an unrelated stretch.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
The number on its own is not a judgement. These are the bands most often used when the result is quoted in a paper, a report or a label:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
0 mismatchesExact motifthe pattern is present as written
1 mismatchConservative hitusually a point mutation or a species difference
2+ mismatchesLoose hitraise the allowance only if you expect divergence

  • X matches any residue, so a pattern full of X matches almost anywhere — count the X positions before trusting a hit.

  • The search is a sliding window over the forward sequence only; report both strands only makes sense for DNA, and this page is for protein.

  • Masses are average residue masses plus one water, the same convention as a peptide mass calculator, so they will be a few hundredths off a monoisotopic mass.

  • Positions are 1-based, the convention in protein databases.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
These are the errors that account for almost every wrong answer people bring to this calculator:

  • Searching a nucleotide sequence with a protein pattern — every window will look like noise.
  • Treating B and Z as literal letters; they are ambiguity codes for Asp/Asn and Glu/Gln.
  • Allowing three mismatches on a six-residue pattern, which matches everything.
  • Comparing a hit's average mass with a monoisotopic mass from a mass spectrometer and expecting them to agree to the last decimal.

faq.q: What does a fuzzy search do that an exact search does not?
faq.a: It lets a pattern match when a few positions differ, and it understands the IUPAC ambiguity letters (B, Z, J, X) that protein databases use.

faq.q: Why do I get a hit in a protein that should not contain the motif?
faq.a: Because you allowed mismatches — check the mismatch count on the hit. With a short pattern and two allowed mismatches, random matches are common.

faq.q: Are the masses monoisotopic or average?
faq.a: Average, using the standard residue masses plus H₂O for the intact peptide. For a mass spectrometry match, compare the monoisotopic mass instead.

faq.q: Can I search several patterns at once?
faq.a: Run them one after another; the page reports every window of the one pattern you paste.

faq.q: What does the Fuzzy Protein Search actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns matches found, fewest mismatches in a hit and residues searched. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.
